questions.q: How does sandboxing differ from the approval checkpoints, stopping conditions, and budgets covered earlier in this course?
options: Sandboxing is just another name for an approval checkpoint
Sandboxing limits what an agent is even capable of doing by constraining its environment and credentials, regardless of what it decides, rather than controlling its decisions directly
Sandboxing only applies to agents that never call any tools
Sandboxing replaces the need for audit logging
questions.explain: Approval, stopping conditions, and budgets govern what the agent chooses to do; sandboxing is a backstop that limits what's structurally possible even if those behavioral controls fail or are bypassed.

questions.q: What does Anthropic's own guidance on building agents list among its concrete recommended safeguards?
options: Removing all system prompts from agent deployments
Extensive testing in sandboxed environments, along with appropriate guardrails
Giving every agent full administrative access by default for simplicity
Avoiding tool use entirely for any production agent
questions.explain: The guidance explicitly recommends sandboxed-environment testing plus appropriate guardrails as a core safeguard for deploying agents, not an optional extra.

questions.q: In the scoped-vs-over-broad API key example, why does the scoped key (refunds:write, orders:read only) provide a stronger guarantee than careful prompting alone?
options: It makes most worst-case outcomes structurally impossible — even if the agent is tricked or makes a mistake, the credential itself can't perform actions outside its scope
It makes the API calls run faster
It eliminates the need for any approval checkpoints
It has no real security benefit over a full-access key
questions.explain: A scoped credential bounds what's possible at the infrastructure level, so even a successful prompt injection or a bug in the agent's logic can't exceed that scope — unlike prompting, which only shapes likely behavior.

questions.q: What does environment isolation (e.g., a sandbox with an egress allowlist and a read-only filesystem) protect against that credential scoping alone does not?
options: It has no distinct purpose from credential scoping
It bounds where a tool's code actually executes — network, filesystem, and system access — so that even a tool working exactly as intended can't reach beyond its sandbox
It only matters for tools that never make any API calls
It replaces the need for cost budgets entirely
questions.explain: Credential scope limits what an agent can reach through APIs it calls; environment isolation limits what its executing code itself can touch (filesystem, network, other processes), covering a different surface.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does Anthropic's phrase "trusted environments" specifically mean as a condition for giving an agent autonomy?
options: An environment where the agent has been told to behave well in its system prompt
Any environment at all, since sandboxing is optional
An environment where sandboxing and credential scoping have already bounded the damage if the agent's behavioral controls fail — a guarantee, not an assumption of good behavior
An environment with no monitoring or logging, to keep the agent unobserved
questions.explain: A trusted environment isn't one where you simply expect good behavior — it's one where sandboxing and least-privilege credentials already guarantee the damage is bounded even if that expectation turns out to be wrong.
